narrative:
The model estimates a 78% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This high probability reflects patterns the system sees in your overall profile compared to others who tend to stay.

Three factors stood out most in the decision. First, having received other job opportunities while at your current employer was the strongest influence pushing the prediction toward leaving. Employees who get external offers are far more likely to depart, and you fall into this group. Second, your total professional experience of 6-10 years also pulled the prediction toward leaving. While this is fairly common (35% of employees predicted to stay have the same range), the model sees it as increasing turnover risk compared to those with only 1-5 years. Third, the amount of time you have spent in your current role (also 6-10 years) worked in the opposite direction, modestly encouraging the model to predict you would stay. Most employees predicted to stay have shorter tenure here, so your longer current tenure slightly counteracted the other signals.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your overall experience outweighed the stabilizing effect of your time in this organization.

The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer promotion paths, better rewards, or addressing your dissatisfaction. You may want to reflect on whether the external opportunities align with your long-term goals. Understanding these drivers can help both sides make more informed choices. (248 words)
